## 1. Purpose

This procedure describes the deployment, retrieval, data management,
and AI-assisted image analysis of camera traps (motion-triggered
wildlife cameras) used in the EA Program. Camera traps provide a
non-invasive method for documenting wildlife presence, activity
patterns, and species richness at field sites. The volume of images
produced by even a small number of cameras (thousands to tens of
thousands per deployment) makes manual review a major bottleneck.
This SOP integrates open-source and cloud-based AI tools to automate
blank-image filtering and species identification, reducing processing
time by an order of magnitude while maintaining scientific rigor
through human-in-the-loop verification.

The EA Program currently uses the CamPark T20 trail camera, but the
deployment and analysis procedures are applicable to other camera trap
models with minor adaptations.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Deployment and image analysis of all EA Program camera
  traps at field sites, including the Bernard Field Station, Pomona
  College Farm, the Pit, and restoration areas
- **Does not apply to:** Live-view video surveillance systems; drone
  imagery (see *SOP-F607*); 360-degree cameras (see *SOP-F89*); aquatic
  camera systems
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites (deployment); EA Program
  laboratory (data analysis)


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve deployment plan, oversee data management |
| Field Lead        | Select camera locations, coordinate deployment and retrieval |
| Trained Personnel | Deploy/retrieve cameras, process images     |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent deployment |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Biological:** Tick and insect exposure, poison oak, snakes at field
  sites. Wildlife encounters when checking cameras in remote locations.
- **Physical:** Uneven terrain, climbing to mount cameras on trees or
  posts. Potential for falls.
- **Security:** Cameras left unattended in public or semi-public areas
  may be stolen or vandalized. Cameras may inadvertently photograph
  people.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Long pants (tick and poison oak protection)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Tick repellent

### Related SOPs

Refer to [SOP-F01 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) for general
field safety procedures.

### Privacy Considerations

Camera traps deployed at sites accessible to the public may capture
images of people. Consult the PI regarding institutional requirements
for signage, data handling, and deletion of images containing
identifiable individuals. Images of people should be deleted during
the initial screening step and never uploaded to public platforms.

## 6. Procedure -- Field Deployment

### 6.1 Camera Setup

1. Install 8 AA batteries in the battery compartment
2. Insert a formatted SD card (Class 10, up to 32 GB)
3. Power on the camera and enter the settings menu
4. Configure the following parameters and record them on the field data
   sheet:

| Setting            | Recommended Value       | Notes                  |
|:-------------------|:------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Photo resolution   | 16 MP                   | Highest available      |
| Video resolution   | 1920 x 1080             | If video is desired; otherwise, photo-only saves battery |
| Trigger mode       | Photo (or Photo + Video) | --                    |
| Photos per trigger | 3 (burst mode)          | Increases detection probability |
| Trigger interval   | 5 seconds               | Balance between captures and battery life |
| Time stamp         | ON                       | Essential for activity pattern analysis |
| Date/time          | Set to current local time | Verify at each deployment |

5. Take a test photo to verify the camera is functioning and the
   timestamp is correct

### 6.2 Site Selection and Mounting

1. Select a location based on the study objectives (game trails,
   water sources, habitat edges, or random/systematic grid points)
2. Record GPS coordinates and camera bearing (compass direction the
   camera faces)
3. Clear vegetation and branches within the camera's detection zone
   (approximately 20 m cone in front of the lens) that could trigger
   false detections
4. Mount the camera at approximately 30--50 cm above ground for
   small-to-medium mammals, or 75--100 cm for larger species
5. Angle the camera slightly downward (approximately 5--10 degrees)
6. Avoid facing the camera directly into the rising or setting sun,
   which causes washed-out images and excessive false triggers
7. Secure with the mounting strap. Apply a cable lock if at a
   public-access site.
8. Walk through the detection zone to verify the trigger is functioning
9. Record the deployment date, time, site ID, camera serial number,
   and SD card number on the field data sheet

### 6.3 Retrieval and Redeployment

1. Navigate to the camera location using recorded GPS coordinates
2. Power off the camera before removing the SD card
3. Remove the SD card and replace with a fresh, formatted card
4. Check battery level; replace batteries if below 50%
5. Power on, verify settings, and take a test photo
6. Record retrieval date, time, and any observations (camera
   displacement, animal damage, vegetation encroachment) on the field
   data sheet
7. Store the retrieved SD card in a labeled case for transport to
   the lab


## 7. Procedure -- Data Management and AI Analysis

### 7.1 Image Download and Organization

1. Insert the SD card into a card reader connected to the lab computer
2. Create a folder following the naming convention:
   `CamTrap_SiteID_CameraID_YYYYMMDD-YYYYMMDD`
3. Copy all images from the SD card to this folder
4. Back up the folder to the external hard drive or cloud storage
   immediately
5. Do not delete images from the SD card until the backup is verified
6. Format the SD card in the camera (not on the computer) before
   redeployment

### 7.2 AI-Assisted Analysis Pipeline

The EA Program uses a two-stage AI pipeline for camera trap image
processing, following the approach used by the Wildlife Insights
platform and the Google CameraTrapAI project [@wildlifeinsights;
@speciesnet2026]:

**Stage 1: Detection (MegaDetector).** An object detection model
identifies whether each image contains an animal, a human, a vehicle,
or is blank (no object of interest). This eliminates the majority of
false triggers and empty frames, which typically constitute 50--90% of
camera trap images.

**Stage 2: Classification (SpeciesNet or similar).** A species
classification model identifies detected animals to the lowest possible
taxonomic level. The model is trained on over 65 million labeled camera
trap images spanning more than 2,000 categories.

### 7.3 Option A: Wildlife Insights (Cloud-Based)

Wildlife Insights is a free, cloud-based platform developed by Google,
WWF, Conservation International, the Wildlife Conservation Society, and
the Smithsonian. It runs both MegaDetector and SpeciesNet automatically
on uploaded images.

1. Create a project at
   [wildlifeinsights.org](https://www.wildlifeinsights.org)
2. Upload images following the platform's batch upload format (images +
   metadata CSV)
3. The platform automatically classifies each image, identifying
   species, count, and confidence score
4. Review AI predictions in the web interface; correct misclassifications
   using the built-in review tools
5. Export the verified dataset as a CSV for analysis in R

::: {.callout-tip}
### Tip
Wildlife Insights filters blank images automatically and achieves
greater than 95% accuracy on well-represented species. Focus manual
review on low-confidence predictions (typically flagged by the
platform) and on species known to be rare or absent from the training
data.
:::

### 7.4 Option B: Local Pipeline (Python)

For projects that require offline processing, greater control, or
cannot upload images to a cloud platform, use the open-source
CameraTrapAI pipeline from Google:

1. Install the CameraTrapAI package from
   [github.com/google/cameratrapai](https://github.com/google/cameratrapai)
2. Run MegaDetector to detect animals and filter blanks:

```bash
# MegaDetector: detect animals, humans, vehicles
python run_detector.py \
  --model_file md_v5b.0.0.pt \
  --image_dir /path/to/CamTrap_SiteID/ \
  --output_file detections.json \
  --threshold 0.2
```

3. Run SpeciesNet on detected animal crops:

```bash
# SpeciesNet: classify species
python run_classifier.py \
  --detections detections.json \
  --model_file speciesnet_v1.pt \
  --output_file classifications.csv
```

4. Review and correct classifications in R or a spreadsheet editor
   (Section 7.6)

### 7.5 Option C: AddaxAI or EcoAssist (Desktop GUI)

For users who prefer a graphical interface over the command line:

- **AddaxAI** ([addaxdatascience.com/addaxai](https://addaxdatascience.com/addaxai/)):
  Desktop application that wraps MegaDetector and SpeciesNet with a
  drag-and-drop interface. Free for researchers.
- **EcoAssist** ([github.com/PetervanLunworX/EcoAssist](https://github.com/PetervanLunworX/EcoAssist)):
  Open-source desktop tool with built-in MegaDetector and optional
  species classifiers. Cross-platform.

Both tools produce output CSVs compatible with the R analysis workflow
below.

### 7.6 Human-in-the-Loop Verification

AI predictions must be verified by a trained observer before use in
analyses or publications:

1. Sort the AI output by confidence score (ascending)
2. Manually verify all predictions below 90% confidence
3. Spot-check a random 10% of predictions above 90% confidence
4. Correct any misclassifications in the output CSV
5. Record the reviewer's name, date, and total number of corrections

::: {.callout-important}
AI models can misidentify rare species, confuse similar-looking species
(e.g., domestic vs. feral cats), or miss cryptic animals in cluttered
backgrounds. Never use unverified AI output for occupancy modeling,
population estimates, or species occurrence records.
:::

### 7.7 Data Analysis in R

```{r}
#| label: camera-trap-analysis
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(camtrapR)  # CRAN package for camera trap data management

# --- Import verified classification data ---
detections <- read_csv("classifications_verified.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    datetime = ymd_hms(timestamp),
    date = as_date(datetime),
    hour = hour(datetime)
  )

# --- Summary statistics ---
cat(sprintf("Total images: %d\n", nrow(detections)))
cat(sprintf("Images with animals: %d\n",
            sum(detections$category == "animal")))
cat(sprintf("Unique species detected: %d\n",
            n_distinct(detections$species[detections$category == "animal"])))

# --- Species accumulation ---
species_by_date <- detections %>%
  filter(category == "animal") %>%
  arrange(datetime) %>%
  distinct(species, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(cumulative_species = row_number())

ggplot(species_by_date, aes(x = date, y = cumulative_species)) +
  geom_step() +
  labs(
    x = "Date",
    y = "Cumulative species detected",
    title = "Species Accumulation Curve"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# --- Activity patterns (diel) ---
activity <- detections %>%
  filter(category == "animal") %>%
  count(species, hour)

ggplot(activity, aes(x = hour, y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~species, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Hour of day",
    y = "Number of detections",
    title = "Diel Activity Patterns"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# --- Detection rate (independent events) ---
# Define independent events as detections of the same species at the
# same camera separated by at least 30 minutes
independent <- detections %>%
  filter(category == "animal") %>%
  arrange(camera_id, species, datetime) %>%
  group_by(camera_id, species) %>%
  mutate(
    time_diff_min = as.numeric(difftime(datetime,
                                         lag(datetime),
                                         units = "mins")),
    independent = is.na(time_diff_min) | time_diff_min >= 30
  ) %>%
  filter(independent) %>%
  ungroup()

# Trap-nights per camera
trap_nights <- detections %>%
  distinct(camera_id, date) %>%
  count(camera_id, name = "trap_nights")

# Detection rate (events per 100 trap-nights)
det_rate <- independent %>%
  count(camera_id, species) %>%
  left_join(trap_nights, by = "camera_id") %>%
  mutate(rate_per_100tn = (n / trap_nights) * 100)

print(det_rate)
```


## 8. Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

### 8.1 Field QC

- Test-fire each camera before leaving the deployment site
- Record all deployment metadata (coordinates, bearing, height, date,
  time, settings) on the field data sheet
- Check cameras at regular intervals (every 2--4 weeks) to replace
  batteries and SD cards
- Log any camera failures, theft, or displacement events

### 8.2 AI Classification QC

- Report the AI model version (e.g., MegaDetector v5b, SpeciesNet v1)
  and confidence threshold used
- Manually verify all predictions below 90% confidence
- Spot-check 10% of high-confidence predictions
- Record the total number and percentage of AI predictions that were
  corrected during verification
- If the correction rate exceeds 10% for a particular species, that
  species' classifications should be fully manually reviewed

### 8.3 Data Reporting

Report the following in any publication or analysis:

- Camera model, settings, and deployment dates
- Number of trap-nights per camera
- AI pipeline used (Wildlife Insights, CameraTrapAI, etc.) with version
  numbers
- Confidence threshold applied
- Verification protocol and correction rate
- Definition of independent detection events (e.g., 30-minute threshold)

## 11. Training Record

Before deploying camera traps independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F01 Field Safety](SOP-F01-field-safety.qmd)
   in full
2. Demonstrate camera setup (batteries, SD card, settings
   configuration, test photo) under supervision
3. Deploy and retrieve at least one camera with proper metadata
   recording
4. Process one SD card through the full AI pipeline (download,
   MegaDetector, SpeciesNet or Wildlife Insights, verification)
5. Produce a verified species list with activity pattern summary
6. Be signed off by the PI or field lead

## Appendix B: AI Tool Comparison {.appendix}

| Feature                 | Wildlife Insights       | CameraTrapAI (Local)    | AddaxAI / EcoAssist     |
|:------------------------|:------------------------|:------------------------|:------------------------|
| Interface               | Web browser             | Python command line      | Desktop GUI             |
| Internet required       | Yes (upload)            | No (after model download) | No (after install)    |
| Cost                    | Free                    | Free (open source)      | Free                    |
| Detection model         | MegaDetector            | MegaDetector            | MegaDetector            |
| Classification model    | SpeciesNet              | SpeciesNet              | SpeciesNet + others     |
| Species categories      | 2,000+                  | 2,000+                  | Varies by model         |
| Batch processing        | Yes (bulk upload)       | Yes (command line)      | Yes (folder selection)  |
| Output format           | Web dashboard + CSV     | JSON + CSV              | CSV                     |
| Human review tools      | Built-in web interface  | External (R, spreadsheet) | Built-in viewer       |
| Data privacy            | Images stored on Google Cloud | Images stay local | Images stay local       |
| Best for                | Standard projects; collaboration | Large datasets; custom pipelines | Users who prefer GUI |
